case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. The exclusion of other plausible etiologies and the regression of clinical and radiological alterations after magnesium replacement therapy support the diagnosis of reversible cerebellar ataxia associated with hypomagnesemia. This patient was taking 2 drugs that can lower magnesium levels: a PPI and a loop diuretic. The use of PPIs impairs absorption of magnesium by intestinal epithelial cells.3The concomitant use of PPIs and diuretics further increases the risk of hypomagnesemia. PPIs were immediately suspended after hypomagnesemia detection. Hypomagnesemia has been detected in up to 12% of hospitalized patients, and in 60% of patients in the intensive care unit setting.4Its clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening arrhythmias, and can include neurological symptoms, hypertension, hipocalcemia, and hypokalemia.5Early neurological disturbances include neuropsychiatric problems and neuromuscular hyperexcitability with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, tremors, fasciculations, and tetany. It can also cause headaches, seizures, fatigue, and malaise.5 Vertical nystagmus is a rare but diagnostically useful sign of severe hypomagnesemia. In the absence of a structural lesion of the cerebellar and vestibular pathways, the only other recognized metabolic etiology is Wernicke encephalopathy.1However, there was no malnourishment, active alcohol use, or evidence of other predisposing conditions associated with Wernicke encephalopathy, and MRI findings were not typical. The lack of a prompt response to intravenous thiamine administration also countered this diagnosis, although the response to thiamine may be less evident in the presence of hypomagnesemia.6 Hypomagnesemia associated with ataxia and reversible cerebellar hyperintensities has been described on a few occasions.7The typical neuroradiological pattern of hypomagnesemia is characterized by cerebellar hyperintense lesions involving the cerebellar vermis. Lesions restricted to cerebellar nodulus are extremely rare. Isolated nodular infarctions are characterized by an abrupt onset of symptoms, typically isolated vestibular syndrome.8The neuroimaging differs from the MRI presented in this patient because of the presence of characteristic diffusion restriction.8 The pathogenesis of cerebellar dysfunction probably relates to the stabilizing role of magnesium on the vascular endothelium. Critically low magnesium levels mimic the vascular endothelial dysregulation seen in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome leading to cerebral edema of the posterior circulation territories.9 Magnesium is not part of the routine electrolyte panel in most hospitals. Hypomagnesemia constitutes a rare and treatable cause of cerebellar ataxia, but one that needs to be specifically thought of. In such cases, early diagnosis and management are essential to avoid permanent cerebellar impairment. Neurologists must be alert to the clinical presentations associated with hypomagnesaemia and the severity of its consequences.

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. The exclusion of other plausible etiologies and the regression of clinical and radiological alterations after magnesium replacement therapy support the diagnosis of reversible cerebellar ataxia associated with hypomagnesemia. This patient was taking 2 drugs that can lower magnesium levels: a PPI and a loop diuretic. The use of PPIs impairs absorption of magnesium by intestinal epithelial cells.3The concomitant use of PPIs and diuretics further increases the risk of hypomagnesemia. PPIs were immediately suspended after hypomagnesemia detection. Hypomagnesemia has been detected in up to 12% of hospitalized patients, and in 60% of patients in the intensive care unit setting.4Its clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening arrhythmias, and can include neurological symptoms, hypertension, hipocalcemia, and hypokalemia.5Early neurological disturbances include neuropsychiatric problems and neuromuscular hyperexcitability with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, tremors, fasciculations, and tetany. It can also cause headaches, seizures, fatigue, and malaise.5 Vertical nystagmus is a rare but diagnostically useful sign of severe hypomagnesemia. In the absence of a structural lesion of the cerebellar and vestibular pathways, the only other recognized metabolic etiology is Wernicke encephalopathy.1However, there was no malnourishment, active alcohol use, or evidence of other predisposing conditions associated with Wernicke encephalopathy, and MRI findings were not typical. The lack of a prompt response to intravenous thiamine administration also countered this diagnosis, although the response to thiamine may be less evident in the presence of hypomagnesemia.6 Hypomagnesemia associated with ataxia and reversible cerebellar hyperintensities has been described on a few occasions.7The typical neuroradiological pattern of hypomagnesemia is characterized by cerebellar hyperintense lesions involving the cerebellar vermis. Lesions restricted to cerebellar nodulus are extremely rare. Isolated nodular infarctions are characterized by an abrupt onset of symptoms, typically isolated vestibular syndrome.8The neuroimaging differs from the MRI presented in this patient because of the presence of characteristic diffusion restriction.8 The pathogenesis of cerebellar dysfunction probably relates to the stabilizing role of magnesium on the vascular endothelium. Critically low magnesium levels mimic the vascular endothelial dysregulation seen in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome leading to cerebral edema of the posterior circulation territories.9 Magnesium is not part of the routine electrolyte panel in most hospitals. Hypomagnesemia constitutes a rare and treatable cause of cerebellar ataxia, but one that needs to be specifically thought of. In such cases, early diagnosis and management are essential to avoid permanent cerebellar impairment. Neurologists must be alert to the clinical presentations associated with hypomagnesaemia and the severity of its consequences.

case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. The exclusion of other plausible etiologies and the regression of clinical and radiological alterations after magnesium replacement therapy support the diagnosis of reversible cerebellar ataxia associated with hypomagnesemia. This patient was taking 2 drugs that can lower magnesium levels: a PPI and a loop diuretic. The use of PPIs impairs absorption of magnesium by intestinal epithelial cells.3The concomitant use of PPIs and diuretics further increases the risk of hypomagnesemia. PPIs were immediately suspended after hypomagnesemia detection. Hypomagnesemia has been detected in up to 12% of hospitalized patients, and in 60% of patients in the intensive care unit setting.4Its clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening arrhythmias, and can include neurological symptoms, hypertension, hipocalcemia, and hypokalemia.5Early neurological disturbances include neuropsychiatric problems and neuromuscular hyperexcitability with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, tremors, fasciculations, and tetany. It can also cause headaches, seizures, fatigue, and malaise.5 Vertical nystagmus is a rare but diagnostically useful sign of severe hypomagnesemia. In the absence of a structural lesion of the cerebellar and vestibular pathways, the only other recognized metabolic etiology is Wernicke encephalopathy.1However, there was no malnourishment, active alcohol use, or evidence of other predisposing conditions associated with Wernicke encephalopathy, and MRI findings were not typical. The lack of a prompt response to intravenous thiamine administration also countered this diagnosis, although the response to thiamine may be less evident in the presence of hypomagnesemia.6 Hypomagnesemia associated with ataxia and reversible cerebellar hyperintensities has been described on a few occasions.7The typical neuroradiological pattern of hypomagnesemia is characterized by cerebellar hyperintense lesions involving the cerebellar vermis. Lesions restricted to cerebellar nodulus are extremely rare. Isolated nodular infarctions are characterized by an abrupt onset of symptoms, typically isolated vestibular syndrome.8The neuroimaging differs from the MRI presented in this patient because of the presence of characteristic diffusion restriction.8 The pathogenesis of cerebellar dysfunction probably relates to the stabilizing role of magnesium on the vascular endothelium. Critically low magnesium levels mimic the vascular endothelial dysregulation seen in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome leading to cerebral edema of the posterior circulation territories.9 Magnesium is not part of the routine electrolyte panel in most hospitals. Hypomagnesemia constitutes a rare and treatable cause of cerebellar ataxia, but one that needs to be specifically thought of. In such cases, early diagnosis and management are essential to avoid permanent cerebellar impairment. Neurologists must be alert to the clinical presentations associated with hypomagnesaemia and the severity of its consequences.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"

       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. The exclusion of other plausible etiologies and the regression of clinical and radiological alterations after magnesium replacement therapy support the diagnosis of reversible cerebellar ataxia associated with hypomagnesemia. This patient was taking 2 drugs that can lower magnesium levels: a PPI and a loop diuretic. The use of PPIs impairs absorption of magnesium by intestinal epithelial cells.3The concomitant use of PPIs and diuretics further increases the risk of hypomagnesemia. PPIs were immediately suspended after hypomagnesemia detection. Hypomagnesemia has been detected in up to 12% of hospitalized patients, and in 60% of patients in the intensive care unit setting.4Its clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening arrhythmias, and can include neurological symptoms, hypertension, hipocalcemia, and hypokalemia.5Early neurological disturbances include neuropsychiatric problems and neuromuscular hyperexcitability with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, tremors, fasciculations, and tetany. It can also cause headaches, seizures, fatigue, and malaise.5 Vertical nystagmus is a rare but diagnostically useful sign of severe hypomagnesemia. In the absence of a structural lesion of the cerebellar and vestibular pathways, the only other recognized metabolic etiology is Wernicke encephalopathy.1However, there was no malnourishment, active alcohol use, or evidence of other predisposing conditions associated with Wernicke encephalopathy, and MRI findings were not typical. The lack of a prompt response to intravenous thiamine administration also countered this diagnosis, although the response to thiamine may be less evident in the presence of hypomagnesemia.6 Hypomagnesemia associated with ataxia and reversible cerebellar hyperintensities has been described on a few occasions.7The typical neuroradiological pattern of hypomagnesemia is characterized by cerebellar hyperintense lesions involving the cerebellar vermis. Lesions restricted to cerebellar nodulus are extremely rare. Isolated nodular infarctions are characterized by an abrupt onset of symptoms, typically isolated vestibular syndrome.8The neuroimaging differs from the MRI presented in this patient because of the presence of characteristic diffusion restriction.8 The pathogenesis of cerebellar dysfunction probably relates to the stabilizing role of magnesium on the vascular endothelium. Critically low magnesium levels mimic the vascular endothelial dysregulation seen in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome leading to cerebral edema of the posterior circulation territories.9 Magnesium is not part of the routine electrolyte panel in most hospitals. Hypomagnesemia constitutes a rare and treatable cause of cerebellar ataxia, but one that needs to be specifically thought of. In such cases, early diagnosis and management are essential to avoid permanent cerebellar impairment. Neurologists must be alert to the clinical presentations associated with hypomagnesaemia and the severity of its consequences.

case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. The exclusion of other plausible etiologies and the regression of clinical and radiological alterations after magnesium replacement therapy support the diagnosis of reversible cerebellar ataxia associated with hypomagnesemia. This patient was taking 2 drugs that can lower magnesium levels: a PPI and a loop diuretic. The use of PPIs impairs absorption of magnesium by intestinal epithelial cells.3The concomitant use of PPIs and diuretics further increases the risk of hypomagnesemia. PPIs were immediately suspended after hypomagnesemia detection. Hypomagnesemia has been detected in up to 12% of hospitalized patients, and in 60% of patients in the intensive care unit setting.4Its clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening arrhythmias, and can include neurological symptoms, hypertension, hipocalcemia, and hypokalemia.5Early neurological disturbances include neuropsychiatric problems and neuromuscular hyperexcitability with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, tremors, fasciculations, and tetany. It can also cause headaches, seizures, fatigue, and malaise.5 Vertical nystagmus is a rare but diagnostically useful sign of severe hypomagnesemia. In the absence of a structural lesion of the cerebellar and vestibular pathways, the only other recognized metabolic etiology is Wernicke encephalopathy.1However, there was no malnourishment, active alcohol use, or evidence of other predisposing conditions associated with Wernicke encephalopathy, and MRI findings were not typical. The lack of a prompt response to intravenous thiamine administration also countered this diagnosis, although the response to thiamine may be less evident in the presence of hypomagnesemia.6 Hypomagnesemia associated with ataxia and reversible cerebellar hyperintensities has been described on a few occasions.7The typical neuroradiological pattern of hypomagnesemia is characterized by cerebellar hyperintense lesions involving the cerebellar vermis. Lesions restricted to cerebellar nodulus are extremely rare. Isolated nodular infarctions are characterized by an abrupt onset of symptoms, typically isolated vestibular syndrome.8The neuroimaging differs from the MRI presented in this patient because of the presence of characteristic diffusion restriction.8 The pathogenesis of cerebellar dysfunction probably relates to the stabilizing role of magnesium on the vascular endothelium. Critically low magnesium levels mimic the vascular endothelial dysregulation seen in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome leading to cerebral edema of the posterior circulation territories.9 Magnesium is not part of the routine electrolyte panel in most hospitals. Hypomagnesemia constitutes a rare and treatable cause of cerebellar ataxia, but one that needs to be specifically thought of. In such cases, early diagnosis and management are essential to avoid permanent cerebellar impairment. Neurologists must be alert to the clinical presentations associated with hypomagnesaemia and the severity of its consequences.

case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. The exclusion of other plausible etiologies and the regression of clinical and radiological alterations after magnesium replacement therapy support the diagnosis of reversible cerebellar ataxia associated with hypomagnesemia. This patient was taking 2 drugs that can lower magnesium levels: a PPI and a loop diuretic. The use of PPIs impairs absorption of magnesium by intestinal epithelial cells.3The concomitant use of PPIs and diuretics further increases the risk of hypomagnesemia. PPIs were immediately suspended after hypomagnesemia detection. Hypomagnesemia has been detected in up to 12% of hospitalized patients, and in 60% of patients in the intensive care unit setting.4Its clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening arrhythmias, and can include neurological symptoms, hypertension, hipocalcemia, and hypokalemia.5Early neurological disturbances include neuropsychiatric problems and neuromuscular hyperexcitability with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, tremors, fasciculations, and tetany. It can also cause headaches, seizures, fatigue, and malaise.5 Vertical nystagmus is a rare but diagnostically useful sign of severe hypomagnesemia. In the absence of a structural lesion of the cerebellar and vestibular pathways, the only other recognized metabolic etiology is Wernicke encephalopathy.1However, there was no malnourishment, active alcohol use, or evidence of other predisposing conditions associated with Wernicke encephalopathy, and MRI findings were not typical. The lack of a prompt response to intravenous thiamine administration also countered this diagnosis, although the response to thiamine may be less evident in the presence of hypomagnesemia.6 Hypomagnesemia associated with ataxia and reversible cerebellar hyperintensities has been described on a few occasions.7The typical neuroradiological pattern of hypomagnesemia is characterized by cerebellar hyperintense lesions involving the cerebellar vermis. Lesions restricted to cerebellar nodulus are extremely rare. Isolated nodular infarctions are characterized by an abrupt onset of symptoms, typically isolated vestibular syndrome.8The neuroimaging differs from the MRI presented in this patient because of the presence of characteristic diffusion restriction.8 The pathogenesis of cerebellar dysfunction probably relates to the stabilizing role of magnesium on the vascular endothelium. Critically low magnesium levels mimic the vascular endothelial dysregulation seen in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome leading to cerebral edema of the posterior circulation territories.9 Magnesium is not part of the routine electrolyte panel in most hospitals. Hypomagnesemia constitutes a rare and treatable cause of cerebellar ataxia, but one that needs to be specifically thought of. In such cases, early diagnosis and management are essential to avoid permanent cerebellar impairment. Neurologists must be alert to the clinical presentations associated with hypomagnesaemia and the severity of its consequences.

case_info.scenario: A 63-year-old man presented with progressive unsteadiness, malaise, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting of 1 month’s duration. He had recently experienced acute pulmonary edema, atrial fibrillation, a tonic-clonic seizure, transient episodes with tetaniform stiffness in both upper limbs, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding caused by gastric angiodysplasia, which was treated with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and argon electrocoagulation. His medical history included alcohol intake of 2 to 4 drinks daily for several years that had stopped 10 years before admission, hypertension, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes, dilated ischemic cardiomyopathy, and a stroke 12 years earlier and recovered without sequelae. His medications included omeprazole, furosemide, atorvastatin, allopurinol, metformin, levetiracetam, and acenocoumarol. Physical examination revealed confusion, dysarthria, appendicular dysmetria with truncal ataxia, and downbeat nystagmus. He was well nourished. Results of blood tests showed a mild creatinine increase of 1.62 mg/dL (normal range, 0.4-1.2 mg/dL; to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4), serum phosphate levels of 2.4 mg/dL (normal range, 2.5-4.5 mg/dL; to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.323), corrected calcium levels of 7.1 mg/dL (normal range, 9.0-10.5 mg/dL; to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.25), and serum magnesium levels of 0.3 mg/dL (normal range, 1.8-2.5 mg/dL; to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.4114). The results of tests for blood cell count, liver function, and thyroid function were normal, as were levels of sodium; potassium; vitamin B12; folic acid; vitamin E; and antinuclear, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, antigliadin, anti–glutamic acid decarboxylase, and anti-transglutaminase antibodies. Cerebrospinal fluid levels were normal, including proteins, glucose, and cell count; polymerase chain reaction for herpes viruses; and enterovirus. Oligoclonal bands (IgG and IgM) were absent, and IgG index was normal. Onconeural and neuronal membrane antibodies were negative in paired samples of cerebrospinal fluid and serum, and included the following: Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, amphiphysin, Ma2, recoverin, SOX1, titin, Zic4, glutamic acid decarboxylase 65,N-methyl-d-aspartate glutamate receptor, contactin-associated protein-like 2, LGT1, γ-aminobutyric acid type B , AMPA1/AMPA2, dipeptidyl-peptidase–like protein 6, and Purkinje cells. Results of whole-body computerized tomography scan and electroencephalogram were normal. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed hyperintensity on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences without reduced diffusion in the cerebellar nodule (Figure).

case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. The exclusion of other plausible etiologies and the regression of clinical and radiological alterations after magnesium replacement therapy support the diagnosis of reversible cerebellar ataxia associated with hypomagnesemia. This patient was taking 2 drugs that can lower magnesium levels: a PPI and a loop diuretic. The use of PPIs impairs absorption of magnesium by intestinal epithelial cells.3The concomitant use of PPIs and diuretics further increases the risk of hypomagnesemia. PPIs were immediately suspended after hypomagnesemia detection. Hypomagnesemia has been detected in up to 12% of hospitalized patients, and in 60% of patients in the intensive care unit setting.4Its clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening arrhythmias, and can include neurological symptoms, hypertension, hipocalcemia, and hypokalemia.5Early neurological disturbances include neuropsychiatric problems and neuromuscular hyperexcitability with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, tremors, fasciculations, and tetany. It can also cause headaches, seizures, fatigue, and malaise.5 Vertical nystagmus is a rare but diagnostically useful sign of severe hypomagnesemia. In the absence of a structural lesion of the cerebellar and vestibular pathways, the only other recognized metabolic etiology is Wernicke encephalopathy.1However, there was no malnourishment, active alcohol use, or evidence of other predisposing conditions associated with Wernicke encephalopathy, and MRI findings were not typical. The lack of a prompt response to intravenous thiamine administration also countered this diagnosis, although the response to thiamine may be less evident in the presence of hypomagnesemia.6 Hypomagnesemia associated with ataxia and reversible cerebellar hyperintensities has been described on a few occasions.7The typical neuroradiological pattern of hypomagnesemia is characterized by cerebellar hyperintense lesions involving the cerebellar vermis. Lesions restricted to cerebellar nodulus are extremely rare. Isolated nodular infarctions are characterized by an abrupt onset of symptoms, typically isolated vestibular syndrome.8The neuroimaging differs from the MRI presented in this patient because of the presence of characteristic diffusion restriction.8 The pathogenesis of cerebellar dysfunction probably relates to the stabilizing role of magnesium on the vascular endothelium. Critically low magnesium levels mimic the vascular endothelial dysregulation seen in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome leading to cerebral edema of the posterior circulation territories.9 Magnesium is not part of the routine electrolyte panel in most hospitals. Hypomagnesemia constitutes a rare and treatable cause of cerebellar ataxia, but one that needs to be specifically thought of. In such cases, early diagnosis and management are essential to avoid permanent cerebellar impairment. Neurologists must be alert to the clinical presentations associated with hypomagnesaemia and the severity of its consequences.

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

His medical history included alcohol intake of 2 to 4 drinks daily for several years that had stopped 10 years before admission, hypertension, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes, dilated ischemic cardiomyopathy, and a stroke 12 years earlier and recovered without sequelae. His medications included omeprazole, furosemide, atorvastatin, allopurinol, metformin, levetiracetam, and acenocoumarol. Physical examination revealed confusion, dysarthria, appendicular dysmetria with truncal ataxia, and downbeat nystagmus. He was well nourished. Cerebrospinal fluid levels were normal, including proteins, glucose, and cell count; polymerase chain reaction for herpes viruses; and enterovirus. Oligoclonal bands (IgG and IgM) were absent, and IgG index was normal. Onconeural and neuronal membrane antibodies were negative in paired samples of cerebrospinal fluid and serum, and included the following: Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, amphiphysin, Ma2, recoverin, SOX1, titin, Zic4, glutamic acid decarboxylase 65,N-methyl-d-aspartate glutamate receptor, contactin-associated protein-like 2, LGT1, γ-aminobutyric acid type B , AMPA1/AMPA2, dipeptidyl-peptidase–like protein 6, and Purkinje cells. case_info.explanation: Magnesium and calcium replacement therapy were started immediately. Thiamine was also administered. Clinical evolution was favorable with progressive improvement of symptoms, normalization of metabolic parameters, and radiological resolution of the MRI abnormalities. The lack of family history and the speed of onset and advanced age suggested acquired ataxia. The recent history of arrhythmia and seizures indicated an extraneurological involvement, and the transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity suggested neuromuscular hyperexcitability. Notably, downbeat nystagmus can be caused by lesions at the craniocervical junction, diseases of the lower brainstem and cerebellum, or metabolic disturbances, including vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or magnesium deficiencies.1Therefore, vitamin deficiencies and ionic alterations were considered as explanations for the cerebellar dysfunction and cardiac dysfunction.2However, neuromuscular hyperexcitability with tetaniform rigidity made ionic disturbances the first diagnostic suspicion because of its association with metabolism of calcium and magnesium. The patient’s history of alcohol use could have been associated with toxic effects or vitamin deficiency–related ataxia, but alcohol intake had stopped more than 10 years earlier. The critically low serum magnesium levels explained the progressive mental disorder and cerebellar ataxia, downbeat nystagmus, transient episodes of tetaniform rigidity, seizures, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia, and general syndrome. The exclusion of other plausible etiologies and the regression of clinical and radiological alterations after magnesium replacement therapy support the diagnosis of reversible cerebellar ataxia associated with hypomagnesemia. This patient was taking 2 drugs that can lower magnesium levels: a PPI and a loop diuretic. The use of PPIs impairs absorption of magnesium by intestinal epithelial cells.3The concomitant use of PPIs and diuretics further increases the risk of hypomagnesemia. PPIs were immediately suspended after hypomagnesemia detection. Hypomagnesemia has been detected in up to 12% of hospitalized patients, and in 60% of patients in the intensive care unit setting.4Its clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic to life-threatening arrhythmias, and can include neurological symptoms, hypertension, hipocalcemia, and hypokalemia.5Early neurological disturbances include neuropsychiatric problems and neuromuscular hyperexcitability with Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, tremors, fasciculations, and tetany. It can also cause headaches, seizures, fatigue, and malaise.5 Vertical nystagmus is a rare but diagnostically useful sign of severe hypomagnesemia. In the absence of a structural lesion of the cerebellar and vestibular pathways, the only other recognized metabolic etiology is Wernicke encephalopathy.1However, there was no malnourishment, active alcohol use, or evidence of other predisposing conditions associated with Wernicke encephalopathy, and MRI findings were not typical. The lack of a prompt response to intravenous thiamine administration also countered this diagnosis, although the response to thiamine may be less evident in the presence of hypomagnesemia.6 Hypomagnesemia associated with ataxia and reversible cerebellar hyperintensities has been described on a few occasions.7The typical neuroradiological pattern of hypomagnesemia is characterized by cerebellar hyperintense lesions involving the cerebellar vermis. Lesions restricted to cerebellar nodulus are extremely rare. Isolated nodular infarctions are characterized by an abrupt onset of symptoms, typically isolated vestibular syndrome.8The neuroimaging differs from the MRI presented in this patient because of the presence of characteristic diffusion restriction.8 The pathogenesis of cerebellar dysfunction probably relates to the stabilizing role of magnesium on the vascular endothelium. Critically low magnesium levels mimic the vascular endothelial dysregulation seen in posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome leading to cerebral edema of the posterior circulation territories.9 Magnesium is not part of the routine electrolyte panel in most hospitals. Hypomagnesemia constitutes a rare and treatable cause of cerebellar ataxia, but one that needs to be specifically thought of. In such cases, early diagnosis and management are essential to avoid permanent cerebellar impairment. Neurologists must be alert to the clinical presentations associated with hypomagnesaemia and the severity of its consequences.
